clue.text: Bird hiding upside down?

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning upside down sends the letters of the thrashing score up the column in reverse

parts.note: a hiding is a thrashing, as in a match lost ten-nil

explanation.surface: A bird hanging upside down to keep out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hiding' looks like concealment, but it is a heavy defeat: a ten-nil scoreline, TEN NIL, which 'upside down' turns over in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The linnet is a small brown finch of European heathland, famous for its song.

clue.text: Knitted wool diehard, if adolescent, encapsulating rotten song by 4

indicators.note: encapsulating means holding something inside, so the rearranged letters wrap around the next piece
knitted wool is worked into a new shape, so these letters are woven into a fresh order

parts.note: food gone rotten has gone off

explanation.surface: A wool garment for a die-hard teenage fan of a band, wrapped round a bad song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knitted' rearranges WOOL DIEHARD IF ADOLESCENT; 'encapsulating' puts OFF (rotten) inside, between FOLLOWER and FASHION. The 4 is 4-down, THE KINKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Dedicated Follower of Fashion is a 1966 hit single by the Kinks, mocking a Carnaby Street dandy.

clue.text: Song by 4, my true love every second in torment, accepting partner having to leave

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the rearranged letters admit the next pieces inside them
letters in torment are twisted and wrung about, so they are rearranged
every second letter of the word love is taken, its second and fourth

parts.note: an ally is a partner in a cause
someone having to leave must go

explanation.surface: A lover's lament: my true love is in agony every moment, with a partner forced to walk out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every second' works on love alone, taking its second and fourth letters; 'in torment' rearranges those with MY TRUE. The 4 is 4-down, THE KINKS.
explanation.definitionFit: You Really Got Me was the Kinks' breakthrough 1964 single, a UK number one.

clue.text: Group is contemplative, pinching cute pink bottoms

indicators.note: pinching means nipping something between, so the verb takes the next letters inside it

parts.note: someone who is contemplative thinks

indicators.note: bottoms are the last letters of the words cute and pink

explanation.surface: Someone deep in thought absently pinching cute pink behinds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottoms' means the last letters of cute and pink, not backsides; 'pinching' lodges them after the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kinks are the London rock band of the Davies brothers, the band behind this puzzle's songs.

clue.text: Ride, e.g. while high on end of jib

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another follows it, so the jumbled letters come after the letter from jib
end of picks the final letter of the word jib
someone high is intoxicated and muddled, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Describing a fairground ride, perhaps one taken while perched at the tip of a crane's jib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' rearranges E G W H I L E into IGWHEEL; 'on' sets that after B, the end of 'jib'.
explanation.definitionFit: A big wheel is the British name for a Ferris wheel, the fairground ride with hanging cars.

clue.text: Battlestar ready for song by 4

parts.note: the word splits into battle, Waterloo where Napoleon fell in 1815, and star, our own sun
set means ready, as in ready, steady, go

explanation.surface: Reads like the sci-fi series Battlestar Galactica, ready to be sung by a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battlestar' must be split into battle and star; ready gives SET as in ready, steady, go. The 4 is 4-down, THE KINKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo Sunset is the Kinks' 1967 single about a London river view, often called their finest song.

clue.text: That's hilarious! A song by 4

parts.note: LOL, laugh out loud, is the texting reaction to something hilarious

explanation.surface: Someone laughing at a song by a band.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 is 4-down, THE KINKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Lola is the Kinks' 1970 hit single about a nightclub encounter in Soho.

clue.text: Missile launchers stand behind this Irish revolutionary?

parts.note: O' begins many Irish surnames, as in O'Brien
Che Guevara was the Argentine revolutionary

explanation.surface: Rocket crews lining up behind an Irish rebel leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The missile launchers are darts players throwing missiles; the question mark admits that Che with an O' prefix becomes an Irish name.
explanation.definitionFit: The oche is the line on the floor that darts players must stand behind when throwing.

clue.text: Short of money, income up I cracked America

indicators.note: something cracked is broken apart, so these letters are reassembled

parts.note: US is the United States of America

explanation.surface: A broke speaker boasts that income rose once they cracked the American market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' looks like breaking into a market, but it signals the rearrangement of INCOME UP I.
explanation.definitionFit: Impecunious is a formal word for having little or no cash, penniless.

clue.text: Brilliant thing read aloud, packed with celebrities

parts.note: a star is a brilliant shining thing in the sky

indicators.note: aloud says a word for read is spoken, giving a near-identical sounding word

parts.note: to read a subject at university is to have studied it

explanation.surface: Something brilliant read out loud at a glittering celebrity event.
explanation.walkthrough: Read means studied (as in reading law); said quickly, studied sounds like studded.
explanation.definitionFit: A star-studded event or cast is one full of famous names.

clue.text: Whistler's subject clear for artist

parts.note: Whistler's Mother is the famous portrait by James McNeill Whistler, and ma means mother
to clear a sum after costs is to net it

explanation.surface: An artist's subject, taken from Whistler's work, made clear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistler' is not someone whistling but the painter of the portrait known as Whistler's Mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Édouard Manet was the French painter of Olympia and Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe.

clue.text: Bum stuck in barrel dislodged from behind

indicators.note: from behind says the hidden letters are read backwards
stuck in says the letters are lodged inside the words barrel dislodged

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone's backside wedged in a barrel, then knocked loose from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Bum stuck' as the definition, but 'stuck in' is the signal that the letters sit inside 'barrel dislodged'; the definition is 'Bum' alone. 'From behind' reverses RELDI.
explanation.definitionFit: A bum, in the sense of a layabout or loafer, is a lazy, workshy person.

clue.text: Stuff bird, having wiped rear

indicators.note: having wiped rear says the last letter of the bird is rubbed out

parts.note: the kite is a bird of prey

explanation.surface: A taxidermist stuffing a bird after cleaning its backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' looks like a verb about taxidermy, but it is a noun: gear.
explanation.definitionFit: Kit is a set of equipment or gear, the stuff you take along.

clue.text: Ten deathless shrouds outside

indicators.note: shrouds means wraps around, so the long word encloses the numeral

parts.note: what is deathless never ends, so it is eternal
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Ten immortal beings wrapped in burial shrouds lying outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrouds' looks like a noun for burial cloths, but it is the verb wrapping X.
explanation.definitionFit: External is an adjective meaning on the outside, exterior.

clue.text: Old bit of silver, bronzer?

definitions.meaning: a sixpence, the pre-decimal British coin once minted in silver
someone who bronzes skin, one who tans; the question mark flags the made-up sense

explanation.surface: An old silver coin, or perhaps a bronzing agent?
explanation.walkthrough: A tanner was British slang for a sixpenny piece, before decimal coinage in 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for the old sixpence coin, and literally one who tans, darkening skin to a bronze.

clue.text: See 2
Close to Oamaru, back in New Zealand, ice finally melted

indicators.note: close to picks the final letter of the town name Oamaru
in says the word for back sits inside the country's abbreviation

parts.note: fro means back, as in to and fro

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the three-letter word ice

explanation.surface: Near the New Zealand town of Oamaru, the ice finally thawed.
explanation.walkthrough: Oamaru is a town on New Zealand's South Island; only its last letter, U, is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfroze is a past-tense verb for thawed out, so it fits melted.

clue.text: See 2
Picture arrangement where leftism fails

indicators.note: a thing that fails breaks down, so the letters collapse into a new order

explanation.surface: A political observation about where left-wing thinking falls down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture' means a movie; 'where' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A film set is the arranged scenery and props where a motion picture is shot.

clue.text: Maltreat heart of vile contemptible type, love not present

indicators.note: the heart of the word vile is its two central letters
not present says that letter is missing from the word

parts.note: a louse is a contemptible person
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A cruel, vile person who mistreats others when love is absent.
explanation.walkthrough: IL from the middle of vile, then LOUSE with its O removed gives LUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ill-use someone is to treat them badly or cruelly.

clue.text: Underworld horse's retracted organ

indicators.note: retracted means drawn back, so the word for horse is reversed

parts.note: a nag is an old horse
a gland is a bodily organ that secretes

explanation.surface: A horse's organ drawn back in, a vet's anatomy note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld' is the criminal underworld, not Hades.
explanation.definitionFit: Gangland is the world of organised crime, the criminal underworld.

clue.text: Identify parent standing for song by 4

indicators.note: in a down entry, standing makes the words rise up the column, reading backwards

parts.note: to name someone is to identify them
pa is father, a parent

explanation.surface: Instructions to name a parent standing in for a band's singer.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 is 4-down, THE KINKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Apeman is a 1970 Kinks single about leaving civilisation for the jungle.

clue.text: Rusty head in duff nail

indicators.note: in places that letter inside the word for duff

parts.note: duff is British slang for useless or bad

indicators.note: head picks the first letter of the word Rusty

explanation.surface: A rusty head on a faulty nail.
explanation.walkthrough: Duff is British slang for broken or no good.
explanation.definitionFit: A brad is a thin flat nail with a small head, used in woodwork.

clue.text: Mysterious sighting unconfirmed initially by government department

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word unconfirmed

parts.note: FO is the Foreign Office, a British government department

explanation.surface: An unverified report of a strange sighting by a government department.
explanation.walkthrough: The FO is the Foreign Office, Britain's ministry of foreign affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A UFO is an unidentified flying object, the classic mysterious thing seen in the sky.

clue.text: Direction of Mongolia from Bhutan or Thailand

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words Bhutan or Thailand, running across them

explanation.surface: A geography question: which way is Mongolia from Bhutan or Thailand?
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' looks like part of the geography, but it signals the letters lifted out of 'Bhutan or Thailand'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mongolia lies due up the map from both Bhutan and Thailand, across China.

clue.text: Motif in rousing song without an echo

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letters of an are removed

parts.note: an anthem is a rousing song
Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A recurring motif in a stirring song that lacks any echo.
explanation.walkthrough: Echo stands for E in the radio alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, ... Echo).
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is a recurring idea or melody, a motif running through a work.

clue.text: Huge thing half going backward, great forward

indicators.note: going backward says those letters are read in reverse
half takes the first four letters of the eight-letter animal

parts.note: an elephant is a huge animal

explanation.surface: A huge thing half reversing while a great player surges forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' is the footballing position, not a direction; ELEP from half of ELEPHANT is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelé, the Brazilian striker, is widely called the greatest attacking footballer ever.

clue.text: See description in code as cryptic

indicators.note: something cryptic is obscure and scrambled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A description written in code, made cryptic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a bishop's see, not the verb: diocesan describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Diocesan is the adjective for a diocese, the district a bishop governs from his see.
